read.title: More than one kind of human
text: Today Homo sapiens is the only human species alive, but it was not always alone. Two hundred thousand years ago and later, several kinds of human lived at the same time. Neanderthals ranged across Europe and western Asia from roughly 400,000 to 40,000 years ago, with brains as large as ours. Denisovans, first recognized in 2010 from DNA in a finger bone found in a Siberian cave, are known from very few remains. On the Indonesian island of Flores, a small human called Homo floresiensis survived until tens of thousands of years ago.

Harari opens Sapiens with this crowded family tree. He uses the word human for every member of the genus Homo, and he describes early Sapiens as a modest animal that only recently climbed to the top of the food chain. That framing, and his claim that the rapid rise left Sapiens anxious and dangerous, is his interpretation.

The evidence itself is more settled. Ancient DNA shows that Sapiens interbred with both Neanderthals and Denisovans: people outside Africa carry roughly 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA, and some Pacific populations carry notable Denisovan DNA. So the stark picture of one species simply replacing the others needs adjustment. Harari presents both an interbreeding theory and a replacement theory, and the genetic findings favor a mix. Reviewers have also pointed out that Harari is a historian, so readers should check the science against specialists.
